aura: The wild part is that hesitating isn't a flaw in speech, it's basically a signalling system — your "um" is quietly telling the other person's brain "stay tuned, something less predictable is coming," which is why even AI is now being taught to fake it.
facts: "Uh" and "um" follow different rules in your brain — one predicts a short pause, the other a longer one.
Voice assistants are engineered to eliminate filler words, but some newer AI systems are now adding fake "um"s back in because flawless speech feels less trustworthy.
Toddlers barely say "um" — the habit actually grows stronger as your vocabulary and reasoning get more complex, not weaker.
Call centre agents are scripted specifically to avoid filled pauses because hesitation is read as incompetence, even though the same pause from a friend reads as thoughtfulness.
hook: That little "uhm" you just typed isn't a glitch in your brain — it's a feature, and it's precisely timed enough that scientists can predict it before you say it.
question: uhm

sections.body: Linguists call "uhm" and "uh" **filled pauses**. Studies going back to the 1950s (and refined heavily since) show these aren't random noise — they show up right before a harder word or a shift in thought, almost like your brain is buying time. "Uh" tends to come before short pauses, "um" before longer ones. Your listener actually uses this: hearing "um" makes people subconsciously expect something less predictable is coming next, so they pay more attention, not less.

Next time you call Zomato or Swiggy support and get a human (not the bot), notice how the agent rarely says "um" — they're trained on scripts with fixed phrases ("I understand your concern, let me check that for you") precisely to avoid the appearance of hesitation, because hesitation reads as incompetence on a support call. Compare that to a friend explaining why they're late — full of "umm"s — and you don't judge them as incompetent, you judge them as thinking. Context changes how we read the same sound.

Voice assistants are deliberately built to *never* produce filled pauses, because early user testing showed people found it unsettling — like the machine was "struggling." Ironically, some newer AI voice systems (like advanced customer-service bots reportedly being tested by companies including in India's fintech and telecom space) are now being trained to insert small "um"s and "let me see"s on purpose, because a flawless instant answer feels robotic and untrustworthy in emotionally loaded conversations — like a bank fraud call.
sections.h: Why Alexa and Siri don't say it

sections.body: Every studied language has some version of this filler — Hindi speakers often use "matlab" or "woh kya hai na," Tamil speakers say "paatheenga," the Japanese say "eto," the French say "euh." The *function* is identical everywhere: buy processing time, hold your conversational turn so nobody interrupts you, and signal "I'm not done, wait." Interestingly, kids under 4 barely use filled pauses — the skill of strategically hesitating develops with language fluency, so ironically, more articulate adults use "um" more, not less, because they have more complex thoughts to buffer.

title: Why do we say 'uhm' when we talk?
